questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to grow your own vegetables at home
Why food prices change so much every season
Threats to the UK's food supply and fixing them
Why British people eat too much red meat
questions.why: They investigate issues affecting UK food production and food security.

questions.q: How does Pippa keep track of where and when food is grown?
options: She reads every food label carefully in shops
She has a kitchen calendar of seasonal food
She only shops at small local farmers' markets
She grows most of her own food in the garden
questions.why: Pippa has a calendar on her kitchen wall showing which fruit and vegetables grow when.

questions.q: How much of its food does the UK import?
questions.why: Neil says the UK imports around 40% of its food.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT mentioned as a problem affecting Britain's food supply?
questions.why: The report lists conflicts, droughts and biodiversity loss, but not a lack of supermarkets.

questions.q: What does climate reporter Mark Poynting say about the government report's conclusions?
options: They are very serious and clear
They are not based on science
questions.why: He says the conclusions are 'quite stark': ecosystem collapse threatens UK national security.

questions.q: Roughly how much of all greenhouse gases come from food production?
questions.why: Pippa says emissions from food production make up around a third of all greenhouse gases.

questions.q: According to Emma Pinchbeck, what produces the most emissions in farming?
options: Having farm animals on the land
questions.why: She says the biggest chunk of emissions comes from simply having livestock on the land.

questions.q: Why does Emma suggest putting something else on the land for every animal removed?
options: To stop people eating so many vegetables
So farmers help fight climate change
To make meat much cheaper for families
To give the remaining animals more space
questions.why: She says this makes farmers 'part of the solution to climate change, not the problem'.
